issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: The denial/minimisation in Magical Thinking sits awkwardly with the very global, entrenched negative self-change appraisals. A patient who mainly copes by telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad would not typically also report such strongly elaborated identity-collapse appraisals unless there were clearer supporting items linking the trauma to guilt/shame; here the combination feels internally strained.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the negative appraisals are missing the expected guilt/responsibility/being dangerous-to-others theme. Instead they focus on global misery and identity change, which is not impossible but is a weak fit to the trauma-specific cognitive content.

vignette:
Javier Morales was a 22-year-old single HVAC technician of Latin American background who came to treatment after months of trying to manage on his own. The event that had changed things happened at work, during a routine service call that he still experienced as anything but routine. He had been working in a cramped mechanical space when a sudden accident led to serious injury to another person. Javier described the moment as fast, chaotic, and impossible to undo: one second he was doing what he thought he was supposed to do, and the next there was someone badly hurt and shouting, and he was left staring at what had happened with the sense that he had failed to stop it. Since then, he had spent a great deal of time going back over the details in his head, replaying every step and every decision, trying to make sense of how it had happened and what he should have done differently. He could not settle on an explanation he found acceptable. What stayed with him most was the conviction that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop it.

In the weeks that followed, Javier began to experience the memory as something oddly separate from him, as though it belonged to another person rather than to his own life. He said that when it came into his mind, it did not feel like a normal recollection but like being forced back into a scene he never wanted to enter again. At times the memory arrived without warning, intruding while he was trying to work, drive, or fall asleep, and he felt powerless to keep it out. Certain sensory details brought it back sharply. He could smell the event in a way that made no sense to other people but made complete sense to him: the sharp, metallic, mechanical odors from the worksite seemed to return all at once when he thought about what happened, and that smell was enough to make his stomach tighten and his chest feel uncomfortable. He found himself physically reacting before he could think, with a sudden rush through his body whenever something reminded him of the injury or the setting in which it occurred.

Javier's day-to-day life gradually narrowed around what felt manageable. He had come to believe that he could no longer trust his own body, especially in moments that required quick reactions or steady hands, and that feeling made ordinary tasks at work feel more threatening than they had before. As an HVAC technician, he could not avoid the practical demands of the job, but he tried to keep himself in what he experienced as a very limited safety zone: familiar places, predictable routes, and situations with as little surprise as possible. Anything that seemed stressful, even mildly so, he started to avoid when he could. He became reluctant to take on extra responsibilities, stay late, or get involved in anything that might add pressure. He also avoided dates and anniversaries connected to the event, tracking the calendar with a kind of dread and noticing how the days leading up to it made him more on edge. At work, silence became especially difficult. If he was in a quiet basement, a shut-off building, or a space where the usual hum of tools and ventilation suddenly stopped, he felt as if something dangerous was about to happen. That unusual quiet made him scan the environment, tense his shoulders, and wait for the next bad moment.

Over time, Javier noticed that he seemed unlike the person he had been before. He spoke of himself with embarrassment and grief, saying the person he had become was unrecognisable to him. He had once thought of himself as capable and dependable, but now he felt altered in a way he could not fully name. The change was not dramatic in how others saw him, but it was vivid to him in private, especially when he compared his current caution and self-doubt with how he had once approached work and daily life. He continued to do his job, but with a narrower sense of ease, and the consequences of his avoidance began to show in his relationships and in the strain of carrying everything alone. He did not want to burden family or friends with the details, yet the effort of holding it in made him increasingly isolated.

By the time he sought help, Javier was exhausted by the loop of remembering, analyzing, bracing, and avoiding. He came because he could no longer tolerate how often the memory forced its way into his mind and because the dates, the silences, and the workplace reminders were making ordinary life feel trapped inside the perimeter of that one day. What frightened him most was the sense that he might remain this way, permanently unable to trust himself, permanently defined by what happened, and what he hoped for most was some way to feel like himself again without having to keep living inside the accident.
